clue.text: Fish ultimately filling wet table, all one wants to buy

indicators.note: a filling sits inside something, so this piece goes into the middle of another

parts.note: sopping means soaked through, very wet

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the last letter of the word
a table of figures or names is a list

explanation.surface: A fishmonger lays out a wet table of fish, and a shopper eyes everything they want.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish' looks like the start of a seafood scene, but only its last letter is used, and 'ultimately' is the selector rather than a sense of finality.
explanation.definitionFit: A written record of every item someone intends to purchase on an errand is exactly what this phrase names.

indicators.note: to tour is to go all the way round something, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: a sow is a female pig
a hall is a large country house

explanation.surface: A shallow pig wanders round a stately home on a guided tour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Large residence' is a country house, the sense of hall in names like Haddon Hall; 'touring' makes the pig go right round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lacking depth of thought or feeling is described as both superficial and shallow; the two adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Sound of animal coming from Fido in kennel

indicators.note: letters coming from a phrase emerge out of its middle, running unbroken across the words

parts.note: the letters run consecutively across the end of the first word, the whole second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A noise comes from the kennel where Fido the dog lives.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface expects a bark from a dog, but the hidden noise is a pig's: fidO IN Kennel gives OINK.
explanation.definitionFit: The grunting noise a pig makes is conventionally written this way, so it is a farmyard animal's call.

clue.text: Sick person? Obvious one needs tucking in

indicators.note: tucking something in pushes it inside a covering, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: patent means plain or evident
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A nurse decides that an obviously ill person needs tucking into bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The scene of a nurse tucking a sick person into bed is the disguise; the tucking puts I inside PATENT, giving PATIENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone receiving medical treatment for an illness is called a patient by doctors and hospitals.

indicators.note: something rewritten is set down again in a new form, so these letters come out in a different order

parts.note: taken as written, seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A note was redrafted without any trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note was rewritten' reads like a message being redrafted; the seven letters rearrange to NO SWEAT.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrase means without effort or difficulty, an idiom used adverbially, as in 'I managed it no sweat'.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to try something with the tongue
second meaning: to beat soundly, as in a contest

explanation.walkthrough: The two words look like the phrase 'taste defeat', meaning to lose, but they are separate meanings of one short verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to pass the tongue over something and, informally, to thrash an opponent in a fight or game.

parts.note: a show is a performance on stage
an event called off is cancelled

explanation.surface: An attention-seeking performer finds that their show has been cancelled.
explanation.walkthrough: The self-promoter's cancelled gig is a sad story, but the two words simply join: SHOW + OFF.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who constantly seeks attention and boasts about themselves is a show-off; self-publicist is a near synonym.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a rick is a sprain or crick, and 'say' marks this as one example of such an ache
second meaning: an annoying, wearisome individual

explanation.surface: Someone called Rick is being described as a bore.
explanation.walkthrough: Rick looks like a man's name, but a rick is a wrenched muscle, the sort of strain that gives a literal ache below the head.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is used for any irritating, tiresome person, while literally it names an ache like a cricked muscle.

parts.note: the surface sense: stylishly turned out and glamorous
the setter's sense: wearing clothes for going out to slaughter game, taken literally

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a literal reading of a fashion idiom: a hunter's gear is clothing worn for the purpose of killing.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone wearing striking, glamorous clothes meant to impress, while the literal words fit a hunter.

clue.text: Hostile to Muslim official, criminal isn't

parts.note: an aga is a commander or chief official in the Ottoman Empire

indicators.note: criminal means crooked or bent, so these letters are twisted out of order

parts.note: the four letters, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone opposed to a Muslim official insists the official is no criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: AGA (also spelt agha) is a crossword regular for a Muslim leader. 'Criminal' looks like a noun but shuffles ISNT.
explanation.definitionFit: To be against something is to oppose it, so the preposition matches 'hostile to', as in 'they were hostile to the plan'.

indicators.note: on the phone you only hear a word, so the spelling must be taken from its sound

parts.note: a sucker is a gullible person, easily fooled

explanation.surface: Someone rings to help a fool over the phone, or to ask for help.
explanation.walkthrough: SUCKER and SUCCOUR sound the same in British speech, where the final R is not voiced.
explanation.definitionFit: Succour is assistance and support given in time of hardship, a formal synonym for aid.

clue.text: African river initially narrows, in leaving Egypt

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each following word gives up its opening letter

parts.note: the first letters of the four words

explanation.surface: A great African river narrows as it flows out of Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' seems to apply only to 'narrows', but it covers all four words. The river is the definition and also flows through the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The longest river in Africa runs north through Sudan and Egypt to the Mediterranean, a famous geographic example.

clue.text: Stage appearing similar from either wing?

parts.note: the definition: a stage or tier in a progression, such as in a game
the instruction: the word reads the same from the left end as from the right

explanation.surface: A theatre stage looks the same viewed from either side of the wings.
explanation.walkthrough: The wings sound theatrical, but here they are the two ends of the word, which mirror each other.
explanation.definitionFit: A stage of progress, like a stage in a computer game or of education, is also called a level.

parts.note: something directed to a target is aimed at it
SS is the abbreviation for steamship

explanation.surface: A missile is launched at a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Launch' suggests a ship being launched, but here it means to throw. SS, for steamship, is a standard abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw or hurl something into the air is to launch it, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Enclosed compartment in back of car, hot

parts.note: in British English the boot is the luggage space at the back of a car (the US trunk)
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Someone shut in a hot compartment at the back of a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back of car' looks like a letter selection, but it defines the whole word BOOT, the British name for a car's luggage space.
explanation.definitionFit: A small partitioned space such as a phone box, polling cubicle or restaurant alcove is called a booth.

indicators.note: coming before means going first, so in this down entry the first piece sits above the other

parts.note: a cub is a young animal, or a junior Scout
taken as written

explanation.surface: A youngster is introduced to someone from an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the last word; the pieces go in clue order: CUB + AN.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Cuba, the largest island in the Caribbean, is an example of someone living on an island.

parts.note: novel as an adjective means new
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: A novel has been left behind somewhere in a British city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book, but it is the adjective. Newport, in south Wales, has city status.
explanation.definitionFit: Newport is a Welsh port granted city status in 2002, making it one example of a city in Britain.

indicators.note: an ending on a word is its final part, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of the word
to ruffle someone is to upset or fluster them

explanation.surface: Someone is upset that a chocolate has ended up trodden into the carpet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like an anagram signal but is a plain synonym, RUFFLE, placed after T.
explanation.definitionFit: A truffle is a rich round sweet made of chocolate ganache, so it is one kind of chocolate.

indicators.note: something ground has been crushed to bits, so these letters are broken up and remade

parts.note: taken as written, seven letters

explanation.surface: Something is lifted to a point just above the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lift near the ground' reads like a physical instruction, but 'lift' means cheer and 'ground' grinds the letters of 'near the'.
explanation.definitionFit: To lift someone's spirits is to encourage or cheer them, which is what hearten means as a verb.

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit within it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: an action or effect is something that takes force, as in 'in action'
U means upper-class, from Nancy Mitford's 'U and non-U' usage

explanation.surface: A sale that is in effect rather posh.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class or posh is a crossword staple. 'In effect' reads like 'effectively' but places U inside ACTION.
explanation.definitionFit: An auction is a public sale where goods go to the highest bidder, so it is one kind of sale.

indicators.note: something on the rocks is wrecked, and to rock is to shake, so these letters are tossed about

parts.note: taken as written, seven letters

explanation.surface: A duck spends a night out on the rocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' wants to be the bird; it is the cricket score of zero. In cricket a batter who is out without scoring is out for a duck.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a duck is a score of zero, so the word stands for nil, a crossword-favourite sense.

clue.text: Praise leaders of urban district brought into fold

indicators.note: bringing something into a space puts it inside, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: a plait is a fold or pleat in fabric

indicators.note: leaders go at the front, so each word gives up its first letter

parts.note: the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: The heads of a town district are praised for bringing people into the fold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fold' suggests a sheep pen or a political flock; here it is a pleat, spelt PLAIT, opened to take UD.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaudit is an expression of approval or applause, so it means praise; the singular matches the noun.

clue.text: Leak fixer observing boards under opening in pipe

indicators.note: in a down entry, a piece under another sits below it, so it comes second
an opening is a beginning, so only the first letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word
lumber is sawn timber, wooden boards

explanation.surface: A tradesman fixing a leak watches the floorboards beneath an open pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: The plumbing scene is apt, which hides that 'pipe' only supplies P, with LUMBER placed below it in the down light.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesperson who installs and repairs water pipes is called on to mend leaks, so the description fits.

clue.text: Face etc rearranged in a manner of speaking

parts.note: a dial is a clock face, and slang for a person's face

indicators.note: rearranged means put in a different order, so the letters next to it are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, three letters

explanation.surface: A face and so on rearranged, in a manner of speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a manner of speaking' looks like a stock phrase meaning 'so to say'; 'manner of speaking' is the definition, and only ETC is shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: A dialect is a regional form of a language, a particular way people talk, hence a manner of speaking.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a small cut or notch
second meaning: a short form of Nicholas

explanation.walkthrough: Mark looks like a boy's name itself, but it means a notch; the answer is another boy's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A notch is a small scratch or cut on a surface, and the same word is a common short form of Nicholas.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: staunch and reliable, as a loyal friend
second meaning: a dark, strong ale such as Guinness

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a recommendation for a reliable pint, but the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means staunch or resolute, as in a stout defender, and the noun is a dark brewed ale.

clue.text: Line of soldiers went quickly for more than half a mile?

parts.note: to run is to go quickly; past tense
K stands for kilometre, which is about 0.62 of a mile

explanation.surface: A line of soldiers ran at speed for over half a mile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More than half a mile' looks like a letter count from 'mile', but it is a kilometre, abbreviated K; the question mark flags the indirect clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A rank is a row of soldiers standing side by side, so the noun names a line of troops.

clue.text: Queen locked out, entrance and exit barred

indicators.note: with both doors blocked nothing can stand at either end, so the word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: someone locked out has been barred or excluded

explanation.surface: A queen is locked out of her palace, with every door barred.
explanation.walkthrough: BANNED loses its B and D to leave ANNE, the queen who reigned 1702-14.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne was Queen of England, Scotland and later Great Britain, the last Stuart monarch, so she is one example.

indicators.note: to house something is to hold it inside, so the letters are contained within the words

parts.note: the letters run consecutively across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A fit, well-to-do Belgravia guest house; Belgravia is a wealthy district of central London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guest houses' looks like a noun phrase, but 'houses' is the verb that holds the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An ague is a feverish fit of shivering, from old usage for malaria, so it is a bout of illness.

clue.text: Greek character turning nose up at Italian drink

parts.note: chi is the 22nd letter of the Greek alphabet
to turn one's nose up at something is to be opposed to it

explanation.surface: A Greek turns his nose up at an Italian wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning' looks like a reversal signal, but the whole phrase is a definition of the piece, meaning opposed.
explanation.definitionFit: Chianti is a red wine from Tuscany, so it is one example of an Italian beverage.

clue.text: Agreement worth millions perhaps that doesn't impress me much

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a large-scale business contract
second meaning: an ironic exclamation dismissing something as unimportant

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs off a multi-million agreement as unimpressive.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half echoes the Shania Twain song title 'That Don't Impress Me Much', and is the sarcastic retort, not a description.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally a major commercial transaction; said sarcastically, the phrase means 'so what?', expressing indifference.

clue.text: Keeping first bit of garbage, man returned rubbish in drawers, say

definitions.note: drawers are plural but name a single garment, and 'say' marks them as one example of the class

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece is held inside the other
rubbish is a mess, so the letters beside it come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, eleven letters

indicators.note: the first bit of a word is its opening letter, which is all that is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A man brings home rubbish stuffed in a chest of drawers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawers' looks like furniture but is underwear. 'Returned' looks like a reversal, but it is part of the fodder, not an indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Drawers is an old word for underpants or knickers, an item of clothing worn beneath outer clothes.
